questions.q: What are the three arguments of the IF function, in order?
options: logical_test, value_if_true, value_if_false
value_if_true, value_if_false, logical_test
criteria_range, criteria, sum_range
condition, and_condition, or_condition
questions.explain: IF always takes the condition first, then what to return if it's true, then what to return if it's false — in that fixed order.

questions.q: How do you get a formula to return more than two possible outcomes using IF?
options: Nest another IF inside the false argument of the first IF, and repeat as needed
Add a fourth argument to IF
Use IF twice in separate, unrelated cells
IF can never return more than two outcomes under any circumstance
questions.explain: Nesting places a second (or third, or fourth) IF inside the false branch of the previous one, letting the chain fall through multiple conditions before landing on a final result.

questions.q: Why does formatting a nested IF with one condition per line and indentation matter, even though Excel accepts it on one line?
options: It makes the formula's logic scannable and debuggable, rather than a single dense string of parentheses
It changes how Excel calculates the result
It is required by Excel's formula syntax rules
It has no real benefit — it's purely cosmetic and never worth the effort
questions.explain: Excel doesn't require any particular formatting, but one-condition-per-line formatting is what makes a nested IF possible to audit and fix later, versus untangling it character by character.

questions.q: Which is a specific sign that a nested IF chain has grown too long?
options: You've lost count of how many closing parentheses the formula needs
The formula uses the word 'IF' more than once
The formula references more than one column
The formula is shorter than 50 characters
questions.explain: Losing track of the closing-parenthesis count is a concrete, practical signal that the nested IF chain has outgrown what's safely maintainable.

questions.q: What should replace a long nested IF where every branch tests the same field against a new ordered threshold (like pricing tiers)?
options: IFS, or a small lookup table with VLOOKUP/XLOOKUP
A second, identical nested IF for redundancy
COUNTIFS
Nothing — that pattern is exactly what nested IF is best suited for, with no better alternative
questions.explain: One field tested against several ordered cutoffs is exactly the pattern IFS (Lesson 11) or a lookup table replaces more cleanly — especially since adding a new tier then means editing a table, not rewriting a formula.
